headline: Paraguay's president quit after a bank collapsed.
summary: Santiago Peña resigned as Paraguay's president on Thursday after Ueno Bank collapsed. The digital bank counted more than 60% of the country's adults as customers and held pensions, and millions lost access to their money. Peña held a stake in a company linked to the bank until last year. The lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him.
cover_answer: Frozen in the bank. Congress voted to pay people back.
table_question: Should the boss quit when something under them goes wrong?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: In a country called Paraguay, a bank that holds people's money broke, and most grown-ups there couldn't get their money out, like a piggy bank with the lid stuck. The president used to own a piece of the company behind the bank, so people got angry, and he quit. The country is working out how to pay everyone back.
5-7.why: Piggy bank with the lid stuck: the money is there, nobody can reach it. At this age that is the story, and 'they're working on it' is the landing.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old reasons from the object in front of them, so the bank is a piggy bank with a stuck lid: the money is in there, and the grown-ups are working on the lid. The president owned a piece of it and quit; nothing about impeachment or prosecutors. Expect "could that happen to our bank?" Say what is true for you.

8-12.script: Ueno, a bank in Paraguay, had most of the country's adults as customers. It collapsed and froze their money, pensions included. President Peña owned part of a company tied to it until last year. He quit, and the lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him anyway. The ship sinks, the captain answers.
8-12.why: Collapse, freeze, vote, resignation: a chain. At nine the captain is the rule.
8-12.why_long: A nine-year-old is working out rules and whether adults follow them, so the script hands them the chain from the bank's collapse to the 78-0 vote, and the captain who answers. The stake he held until last year makes the fairness call concrete. Expect "did he know it would break?" Nobody has shown that. Three cases are open.

13-17.script: Peña quit rather than be removed. The opposition says that's the point: an ex-president can be a senator for life, with legal protections, and three cases are open. Should quitting close that door? Second: a bank tied to him had 60% of adults. Who was watching?
13-17.why: Quitting and being removed look the same and aren't. At 16 they can hold the two and see why the opposition cares which.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can reason about what is not in front of them, so the script gives them the gap between resigning and being removed: the same empty chair, different protection afterward. Then it widens to oversight, a question with no villain yet. Expect "why would his own party dump him?" It would rather lose him than own the bank.

5-7.q: Will the people get their money back?
5-7.a: Paraguay's congress agreed on a way to pay people back. It will take a while.

8-12.a: Still in the bank, frozen. Congress approved a way to pay people back.
Nobody has shown that. Prosecutors are looking. He denies wrongdoing.

13-17.q: Why does resigning matter if he's out either way?
13-17.a: Senator for life comes with legal protections. Removal might not.

13-17.q: How does one bank get 60% of a country?
13-17.a: Obscure five years ago, then a household name. Paraguayans ask the same.
